angle: Volume for volume's sake worked in 2022. Here's what works now.
post_first_line: 8 minutes. That's how long Zach Herman's flow took.
linkedin_post:
8 minutes. That's the whole flow.

Zach Herman says the flow takes maybe 8 minutes total, sometimes less. That time now goes to running more volume, focusing on mid-funnel deals, and working with reps on enablement.

Volume for the sake of volume worked in 2022. Zach loaded up Outreach and sent 1,000 emails a day out of a primary mailbox. It worked great.

That doesn't work today.

What works now is quality volume at scale. Personalization at scale comes up constantly, and Zach sees this flow as the way to actually accomplish it. The quality of the outreach stays very high throughout.

The old playbook was about sending more. The new one is about keeping quality high while sending a lot.

Where are you spending the time you save?

lesson.title: Quality Volume Beats Volume for Volume's Sake
takeaways: Blasting 1,000 emails a day from one mailbox worked in 2022 but doesn't work today.
The goal now is quality volume at scale, with personalization built into the process.
A faster end-to-end flow gives time back for mid-funnel deals and rep enablement.
lesson.exercise: Time your current outreach flow from start to finish. Pick one step that could be streamlined, then decide where you'd spend the saved time, such as mid-funnel deals or coaching reps.

caption: Volume alone stopped working

angle: I tried stitching ChatGPT and Claude into my outbound. It was worse than doing it by hand.
post_first_line: Outbound used to eat 10 to 12 hour days.
linkedin_post:
Outbound used to eat 10 to 12 hour days.

Zach Herman tried a different fix first, and it backfired.

Zach stitched ChatGPT and Claude together to make outbound easier. The output was not even remotely as good as what Zach was doing by hand.

So Zach kept doing it by hand. That meant longer days spent writing stronger emails and making more targeted calls.

Now work that used to take a ton of time takes Zach a couple of minutes. The quality stays strong, and the process picks up on almost all of Zach's context.

The lesson: speed was never the hard part. Keeping quality while saving time was.

A stack of disconnected tools can be faster and still worse. Context is what made the difference.

What did you stop automating because quality dropped?

lesson.title: Faster outbound only counts if quality holds
takeaways: Stitching separate AI tools together can produce output worse than manual work.
Time saved means nothing if email and call quality drop.
Carrying your context into the process is what keeps quality strong.
lesson.exercise: Take one outbound task you do by hand, like writing a first email. Run it through your current automated setup and compare the two side by side. Note what context the automated version missed.

caption: Stitching AI tools made it worse

angle: The 17-title Boolean search SDRs still run, and what replaced it
linkedin_post:
17 titles in one Boolean search.

Zach Herman used to take 25 accounts and run each one individually through LinkedIn Sales Navigator, with a long Boolean string and a lot of hoping for the best.

If the results looked thin, Zach ran the search again. Then the contacts had to be pushed back to ZoomInfo, and the whole process started over.

The new version looks different. Zach took the top 10 contacts from the list to keep it simple, and the suggestions came back automatically.

From there, the list can be ranked on whatever matters. Funding amount. How many jobs a company is hiring for. Something as specific as more than 200 open jobs and a Series C raised in the last 3 months.

The work shifted from digging for contacts to deciding what makes an account worth calling first.

What's the longest Boolean string you've ever written?

Slide 2: Zach Herman ran this on 25 accounts, one at a time.
Slide 3: Thin results meant running the search all over again.
Slide 4: Then the contacts got pushed back to ZoomInfo.
Slide 5: The new way starts with the top 10 contacts per list.
Slide 6: Suggestions show up without writing a single Boolean string.
Slide 7: Rank by funding amount or number of open jobs.
Slide 8: Example: 200+ jobs open and a Series C in 3 months.

lesson.title: Stop hunting for contacts, start ranking accounts
takeaways: Long Boolean searches across many titles are slow and unreliable, and often need to be repeated.
Moving contacts between tools adds steps that rebuild the same process each time.
Ranking on specific criteria like funding amount or hiring volume tells reps where to focus first.
lesson.exercise: Pick one account list you work this week. Write down two criteria, such as funding stage and open jobs, that would make an account a priority, then rank the list on them before pulling any contacts.

angle: I tried ChatGPT as an SDR and it made my outreach slower, not faster
post_first_line: Zach Herman tried ChatGPT as an SDR. Outreach got slower.
linkedin_post:
Zach Herman tried ChatGPT as an SDR. Outreach got slower.

The tool wasn't the problem. The fit was.

This was around 2022, '23, when the first version of ChatGPT came out. The stack was already full: Outreach, ZoomInfo, Sales Navigator, Six Sense, Demandbase. Then AI got thrown into the mix and everybody tried to use it effectively.

Zach tried to get it to write better basic copy. It couldn't remember who Zach was or how Zach talks.

So every draft took more time to coax into shape. Getting the tool to write the way Zach wanted took longer than just writing it. Zach ended up back to doing it manually.

The lesson: a general-purpose AI tool isn't built for sellers. If it doesn't know your voice, you're editing instead of selling.

When did an AI tool last cost you time?

Slide 2: Around 2022, '23, the first ChatGPT version landed on top of a full stack.
Slide 3: Outreach, ZoomInfo, Sales Nav, Six Sense, Demandbase were already in the mix.
Slide 4: The goal was simple: write better basic copy, faster.
Slide 5: But it couldn't remember how Zach actually talks.
Slide 6: Coaxing the tool took longer than writing the message.
Slide 7: So Zach went back to writing outreach manually.
Slide 8: General AI isn't built for sellers. Fit matters more than hype.

lesson.title: When AI Slows You Down
takeaways: A tool that isn't purpose-built for sellers can add work instead of removing it.
If AI can't remember your voice, you spend your time editing and re-prompting.
Speed gains only count if the total time to a sendable message drops.
lesson.exercise: Time yourself writing five outreach messages with your AI tool and five by hand. Compare total time to a message you'd actually send.

caption: AI made outreach slower

angle: The 6-tool prospecting workflow most AEs are a little embarrassed to admit they used to run
post_first_line: Six tools just to send one email.
linkedin_post:
Six tools just to send one email.

Speaker D admits the old prospecting workflow is a little embarrassing to look back on.

It went like this: build an account report in Salesforce. Open LinkedIn Sales Nav to find prospects at those accounts and create a list. Use ZoomInfo to import that list into Salesforce. Go back to Salesforce. Add the people to Outreach. Build a sequence in Outreach. Then finally get the emails out.

Because the process was so long, personalization took a back seat. The result was a spray and pray strategy, with far less tailoring than the outreach deserved.

Speaker D points out that this is probably what a lot of people were doing. It wasn't a one-off mistake. It was the standard playbook.

The lesson isn't that reps were lazy. The process itself made good outreach nearly impossible, because every extra handoff ate time that should have gone into research and personalization.

Speaker D says things are in a much better spot now.

How many steps are in your prospecting workflow today?
carousel: Slide 1: Six tools just to send one email.
Slide 2: Step one: build an account report in Salesforce.
Slide 3: Step two: find prospects and build a list in Sales Nav.
Slide 4: Step three: import that list through ZoomInfo, back into Salesforce.
Slide 5: Step four: add people to Outreach and build a sequence.
Slide 6: The process was so long that personalization got skipped.
Slide 7: Spray and pray became the default, not the choice.
Slide 8: Speaker D says teams are in a much better spot now.

lesson.title: When the workflow kills personalization
takeaways: A long chain of tools leaves less time for personalization, even when reps want to do it.
Spray and pray is often a symptom of a slow process, not a lack of effort.
Many teams ran this same workflow, so admitting it is the first step to fixing it.
lesson.exercise: Write down every tool and handoff between picking an account and sending the first email. Circle the steps that add no personalization, then cut or combine one this week.

caption: Six tools for one email

angle: Strategic account research used to take weeks. I built a full plan and sequence in 3 minutes.
post_first_line: 3 minutes. One full outbound plan and sequence.
linkedin_post:
3 minutes. One full outbound plan and sequence.

It used to take weeks to get there.

Zach Herman used to work strategic accounts as an SDR. Just sending one email meant hours of research and reading 10K reports.

You could spend weeks figuring out who to reach out to at Nike and how to tee it up.

In a recent demo, Zach built a full outbound plan and a sequence for Airbnb in about 3 minutes. Then pushed the contacts straight into the sequence after one more once-over.

Teams using this end-to-end workflow have told us they go from list to sequence 90% faster.

The gain isn't just speed on one step. It's removing the handoffs between research, contacts, and sequencing.

When was the last time research stalled your outreach?

The biggest speed gain comes from an end-to-end workflow, not from speeding up one step.
Keep a human review before contacts go into the sequence.
